Sign / phenotype feature: New or progressive persistent proteinuria
Direction for AA: Strongly supports AA in inflammatory context
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Often the clinical transition that prompts evaluation
Population / context: Patient with a credible AA-driving inflammatory/infectious condition
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Proteinuric kidney disease is the dominant renal presentation across major AA cohorts and guidelines.
Why it matters for suspicion: This is the most practically useful shift from 'AA risk' to 'possible organ involvement'.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: AL and other renal amyloid types also cause proteinuria; diabetic, hypertensive, and primary glomerular disease are common alternatives.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Credible inflammatory driver + persistent inflammatory burden + new/progressive proteinuria
Threshold / criterion status: No universal AA screening cutoff. >0.5 g/24 h was used as a kidney-biopsy referral threshold in one FMF study, not validated across all AA-risk populations.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: proteinuria; UPCR; UACR; 24-hour urine protein
Recommended use in phenotype model: Core trigger; use trend and persistence rather than one measurement.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Renal phenotype disproportionate to or not fully explained by known diabetes, hypertension, medications, or other kidney disease
Direction for AA: Strongly supports AA when inflammation is present
Population / context: High-risk inflammatory disease with a new renal phenotype
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Guidelines emphasize suspicion when new renal manifestations appear in chronic inflammation; no evidence supports excluding patients simply because diabetes or hypertension is also present.
Why it matters for suspicion: Combining precursor state + inflammatory burden + renal transition is more discriminating than any single feature.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Competing renal causes can coexist with AA; apparent 'explanation' by diabetes/HTN may delay recognition.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: AA-driving condition + persistent inflammation + proteinuria ± hypoalbuminemia ± eGFR decline that is new, rapidly progressive, or disproportionate
Threshold / criterion status: Do NOT require 'no diabetes' or 'no hypertension'. Competing causes lower specificity but should not hard-exclude AA.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: diabetes; hypertension; CKD etiology; proteinuria trend
Recommended use in phenotype model: Core composite phenotype. Model competing causes as down-weights/uncertainty, not binary exclusions.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) / periodic fever syndrome
Population / context: Known FMF; Mediterranean/Middle Eastern ancestry may increase prior probability but is not required
Quantitative / comparative evidence: FMF is a canonical AA precursor. In a 2,246-patient Turkish multicenter cohort, biopsy-proven amyloidosis was present in 8.6%.
Why it matters for suspicion: Among the four major systemic amyloid types, FMF is unusually informative for AA because sustained innate-inflammatory activity directly drives SAA production.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: FMF does not make proteinuria synonymous with AA; non-amyloid kidney disease is common enough to require a renal differential.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: FMF + uncontrolled/subclinical inflammation + new persistent albuminuria/proteinuria
Threshold / criterion status: No single FMF duration threshold. Surveillance should focus on inflammatory control and renal change.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: FMF; recurrent fever; serositis; erysipelas-like erythema; periodic fever
Recommended use in phenotype model: Strong background-risk feature; never convert directly to an AA diagnosis.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Other chronic autoinflammatory syndromes (e.g., TRAPS, CAPS, MKD/HIDS)
Population / context: Known monogenic/autoinflammatory disease
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Systematic review of AA causes and contemporary reviews identify multiple periodic-fever/autoinflammatory disorders as strong AA-associated diseases.
Why it matters for suspicion: These conditions create persistent SAA exposure and are much more subtype-oriented toward AA than AL or ATTR.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Rare diseases; coding may be incomplete; renal disease still needs independent evaluation.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Autoinflammatory diagnosis + persistent inflammatory activity + new albuminuria/proteinuria
Threshold / criterion status: No universal duration threshold across syndromes.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: TRAPS; CAPS; MKD; HIDS; autoinflammatory syndrome
Recommended use in phenotype model: Strong background feature; combine with renal transition.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Chronic/active infection (e.g., tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, osteomyelitis, chronic suppurative disease)
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Can precede renal disease by months to years
Population / context: Persistent or recurrent infection with sustained inflammatory burden
Quantitative / comparative evidence: AA cause reviews identify chronic infections as major drivers. In a 43-patient PTB renal-AA cohort, illness duration was <5 years in 93% (mean 2.25 years), showing that very long latency is not required.
Why it matters for suspicion: Prevents a screen from assuming AA only follows decades of rheumatic disease.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Acute/short-lived infection is not equivalent to a chronic amyloidogenic inflammatory state; CKD/proteinuria may have other infectious or drug-related causes.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Persistent infection + inflammatory burden + new proteinuria/edema/renal dysfunction
Threshold / criterion status: Do not impose a minimum multi-year duration. The TB cohort is disease-specific and selected; its 2.25-year mean is not a general AA latency rule.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: tuberculosis; bronchiectasis; osteomyelitis; chronic infection; suppuration
Recommended use in phenotype model: Strong risk context when chronicity/recurrence or ongoing inflammatory activity is documented.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Nephrotic-range proteinuria / nephrotic syndrome
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Often at or near diagnosis; may represent later disease
Population / context: Chronic inflammatory/infectious disease
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome are common in renal AA cohorts; in the FMF biopsy cohort, amyloid kidney disease had much heavier proteinuria than non-amyloid kidney disease.
Why it matters for suspicion: Strong evidence of a glomerular protein-losing process and highly concerning in the right inflammatory context.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: AL is also a major cause of nephrotic amyloid kidney disease; primary glomerular disease remains common.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Nephrotic proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia/edema + chronic inflammatory driver
Threshold / criterion status: Use standard nephrotic definitions (commonly ?3–3.5 g/day depending source); this threshold is not AA-specific.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: nephrotic syndrome; UPCR; 24h urine protein
Recommended use in phenotype model: Very strong organ trigger, but subtype must remain context-dependent.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Persistently elevated serum amyloid A (SAA), when measured for inflammatory disease monitoring
Pre-test usability: Only if ordered independently of amyloid work-up
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Before or after diagnosis depending why it was ordered
Population / context: FMF/autoinflammatory or other chronic inflammatory disease where SAA is routinely followed
Quantitative / comparative evidence: In 374 established AA patients, median SAA was 7 mg/L when deposits regressed versus 54 mg/L when burden increased; <10 mg/L during follow-up was associated with regression in many patients.
Why it matters for suspicion: SAA is the direct fibril precursor and a strong measure of ongoing amyloidogenic inflammatory exposure.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: SAA elevation does not demonstrate tissue amyloid and can be acutely elevated without AA.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: High-risk disease + persistently elevated SAA + new renal protein loss
Threshold / criterion status: IMPORTANT: <10 mg/L is principally a treatment/control target in established disease/FM F guidance, not a validated universal pre-test diagnostic cutoff. Do not trigger AA solely at SAA >10.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: serum amyloid A; SAA
Recommended use in phenotype model: High-value burden feature if already available; model as continuous/longitudinal rather than a binary >10 threshold.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: New microalbuminuria / low-grade albuminuria
Population / context: High-risk chronic inflammatory/autoinflammatory disease under routine follow-up
Quantitative / comparative evidence: FMF renal literature recognizes microalbuminuria as an early renal warning; progression to overt proteinuria is a classic AA pathway.
Why it matters for suspicion: May identify the renal transition before late nephrotic disease.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Diabetes, hypertension, obesity, exercise, infection, and many kidney diseases cause low-grade albuminuria.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: New/persistent albuminuria + active inflammatory driver + upward trend over time
Threshold / criterion status: UACR 30–300 mg/g is the standard microalbuminuria range, not an AA-specific threshold.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: UACR; urine albumin; microalbumin
Recommended use in phenotype model: Early warning feature; require persistence and inflammatory context.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Inflammatory bowel disease, especially aggressive/fistulizing Crohn disease
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Usually after years of active disease, but variable
Population / context: Crohn disease > ulcerative colitis; especially fistulae, abscesses, stricturing disease, repeated surgery
Quantitative / comparative evidence: In a specialist series of 26 IBD-AA patients, 22 had Crohn disease; fistulae/abscesses occurred in 10, and proteinuric renal dysfunction occurred in all cases.
Why it matters for suspicion: An aggressive suppurative Crohn phenotype creates sustained inflammatory burden and is more informative than an IBD diagnosis alone.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: IBD itself can cause diarrhea, hypoalbuminemia, anemia, and renal abnormalities; those findings are not automatically amyloid manifestations.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Fistulizing/abscess-forming Crohn + persistent inflammation + new proteinuria or renal dysfunction
Threshold / criterion status: No validated 'fistula count' or disease-duration threshold. Treat anatomy/behavior as a risk modifier.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: Crohn disease; fistula; perianal abscess; stricturing; bowel resection
Recommended use in phenotype model: Use Crohn phenotype severity as a background modifier; renal transition remains the key trigger.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Delayed diagnosis, inadequate control, or poor colchicine adherence in FMF
Population / context: Known FMF
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Delay in FMF diagnosis is associated with amyloidosis in large cohort data. Historical data summarized in contemporary review show proteinuria developing far more often in colchicine-noncompliant than compliant FMF patients.
Why it matters for suspicion: AA risk depends on cumulative inflammatory exposure; treatment history helps distinguish a well-controlled remote FMF diagnosis from ongoing amyloidogenic exposure.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Medication lists do not prove adherence; 'colchicine resistant' disease can actually reflect non-adherence.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: FMF + recurrent attacks/persistent SAA or CRP + delayed/inadequate colchicine treatment + new renal signal
Threshold / criterion status: No universal adherence percentage or attack-frequency threshold should be hard-coded from retrospective studies.
Likely EHR location: Medication history; rheumatology notes; pharmacy if available
Example structured fields / NLP terms: colchicine; missed doses; nonadherence; resistant; recurrent attacks
Recommended use in phenotype model: Longitudinal risk modifier; use only with evidence of continued inflammatory activity.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Rising creatinine / falling eGFR / kidney failure
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Often later than proteinuria, but may be present at detection
Population / context: Chronic inflammatory/infectious disease
Quantitative / comparative evidence: In the Japanese nationwide survey, 46.2% had moderate/severe renal dysfunction at diagnosis; renal dysfunction dominated the 374-patient natural-history cohort.
Why it matters for suspicion: Substantially increases concern once the inflammatory context and proteinuric pattern are established.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Diabetes, hypertension, nephrotoxins, obstruction, sepsis, and other nephropathies commonly cause eGFR decline.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Progressive proteinuria + falling eGFR + sustained inflammatory burden
Threshold / criterion status: No AA-specific eGFR threshold; trend and unexplained/disproportionate decline matter.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: creatinine; eGFR; CKD; renal failure
Recommended use in phenotype model: Strong contextual feature; not subtype-specific alone.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Recurrent skin/soft-tissue infection, chronic wounds, or repeated abscesses
Data type / source: Diagnosis / medical history / wound care history
Population / context: Patients with chronic/recurrent SSTI, including but not limited to people who inject drugs
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Systematic review of injecting-related AA found SSTI in 88.7% of reported AA cases among people who inject drugs.
Why it matters for suspicion: Captures a chronic suppurative inflammatory pathway that may be missed by rheumatology-centric rules.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Injection-drug-use status itself is not AA evidence; many SSTIs are isolated and self-limited.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Repeated abscess/cellulitis/chronic ulcer + persistent inflammation + new proteinuria
Threshold / criterion status: No validated number of infections/ED visits. Use recurrence/chronicity qualitatively or derive candidate thresholds for validation.
Likely EHR location: ED; wound care; dermatology; problem list
Example structured fields / NLP terms: abscess; cellulitis; chronic ulcer; wound infection
Recommended use in phenotype model: Use the infection burden, not the social label, as the feature.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Recurrent inflammatory flares or persistently uncontrolled precursor disease
Population / context: RA/SpA, FMF, Crohn disease, chronic infection, autoinflammatory disease
Quantitative / comparative evidence: AA progression and outcomes correlate with persistent SAA exposure; modern reviews emphasize suppression of the underlying inflammatory disease as the central preventive strategy.
Why it matters for suspicion: Cumulative inflammatory exposure is mechanistically closer to AA risk than disease duration alone.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Flare coding can be inconsistent and treatment escalation may reflect physician preference rather than severity.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Repeated flares + persistent CRP/SAA + new renal signal
Threshold / criterion status: No validated universal number of flares, steroid bursts, or biologic changes.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: flare; uncontrolled; steroid burst; biologic escalation; resistant disease
Recommended use in phenotype model: Longitudinal modifier; derive candidate burden features for validation rather than a hard rule.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Known chronic inflammatory joint disease (RA, spondyloarthritis, other persistent inflammatory arthritis)
Population / context: Persistent inflammatory joint disease, especially active or historically severe disease
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Inflammatory-joint-disease AA prevalence has fallen markedly in the biologic era; the 2025 systematic review reports older RA prevalence estimates of 16.7–25.2% versus ~0.7% in post-2010 data.
Why it matters for suspicion: AA requires a sustained inflammatory precursor state; a rheumatic diagnosis is therefore meaningful context, but modern treatment substantially changes risk.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: RA/SpA are common and most patients never develop AA. Renal disease may be diabetic, hypertensive, drug-related, glomerular, or AL.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Inflammatory joint disease + persistent inflammatory activity + new albuminuria/proteinuria
Threshold / criterion status: No universal disease-duration, deformity, or Steinbrocker threshold is validated for current pre-test screening.
Likely EHR location: Problem list; rheumatology notes; medication history
Example structured fields / NLP terms: rheumatoid arthritis; ankylosing spondylitis; inflammatory arthritis; biologic escalation
Recommended use in phenotype model: Context feature only; raise weight when ongoing inflammatory burden and a new renal phenotype coexist.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Peripheral edema / anasarca
Population / context: Especially when accompanied by proteinuria/hypoalbuminemia
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Pedal edema was part of the presenting phenotype in the PTB renal-AA cohort and is a standard manifestation of nephrotic protein loss.
Why it matters for suspicion: Visible clinical clue that can appear before formal amyloid investigation.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Heart failure, liver disease, venous insufficiency, drugs, and malnutrition are common causes.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Edema + proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + inflammatory driver
Threshold / criterion status: No specific edema grade is validated for AA.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: edema; leg swelling; anasarca
Recommended use in phenotype model: Supporting renal-cluster feature.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Selected inflammatory neoplastic drivers (especially Castleman disease; also RCC and some other tumors)
Evidence class: Systematic review + disease review + case series
Population / context: Castleman disease; renal cell carcinoma; selected inflammatory malignancies; rare hepatocellular adenoma association
Quantitative / comparative evidence: AA cause review identifies selected neoplasms as strong/recognized associations. In unicentric Castleman case series, resection suppressed inflammation and was followed by regression of AA deposits.
Why it matters for suspicion: Prevents a screen from equating AA exclusively with rheumatologic or infectious disease.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Most cancers are not strong AA drivers; cancer can cause proteinuria, CKD, weight loss, and inflammation by many other mechanisms.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Selected inflammatory tumor + persistently elevated inflammatory markers + new renal protein loss
Threshold / criterion status: No broad 'any cancer' rule. Use a curated list of literature-supported tumor drivers.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: Castleman disease; renal cell carcinoma; RCC; inflammatory tumor
Recommended use in phenotype model: Moderate background feature; stronger for Castleman than for nonspecific malignancy.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Hypoalbuminemia accompanying renal protein loss
Population / context: Proteinuric inflammatory patient
Quantitative / comparative evidence: PTB-associated renal AA cohort reported hypoalbuminemia in 76.7%; low albumin is also common in nephrotic AA.
Why it matters for suspicion: Reinforces a protein-losing renal phenotype and helps separate trivial albuminuria from clinically significant glomerular disease.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Inflammation, malnutrition, liver disease, protein-losing enteropathy, and IBD can lower albumin without AA.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Proteinuria + falling serum albumin + edema + inflammatory driver
Threshold / criterion status: No AA-specific albumin cutoff. Interpret as a trajectory and alongside urine protein.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: serum albumin; hypoalbuminemia
Recommended use in phenotype model: Supporting renal-cluster feature.
Ranking interpretation: AA-supportive feature ranked using suspicion strength, subtype discrimination, evidence quality, pre-test usability, EHR detectability, and actionability.

Sign / phenotype feature: Family history of AA amyloidosis or end-stage kidney disease in FMF
Population / context: Patients with FMF or a convincing periodic-fever phenotype
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Family history of amyloidosis and ESRD was significantly more prevalent among FMF patients with amyloidosis in the 2,246-patient multicenter study.
Why it matters for suspicion: Captures inherited/background susceptibility not represented by the patient's current flare count alone.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Family history may be incomplete or nonspecific; ESRD can have many causes.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: FMF + family history of AA/ESRD + inadequate inflammatory control + new albuminuria

Recommended use in phenotype model: Moderate risk modifier; useful for prioritization but not sufficient alone.

Sign / phenotype feature: Known high-risk MEFV genotype, especially M694V homozygosity, in a patient with FMF
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Known before renal disease if FMF genotyping already performed
Population / context: Patients with established FMF and prior MEFV testing
Quantitative / comparative evidence: In the 2,246-patient Turkish cohort, M694V homozygosity was associated with ~6-fold higher odds/risk of amyloidosis versus other genotypes; pooled Turkish data also support the association.
Why it matters for suspicion: Genotype can refine risk within FMF and may justify closer surveillance when combined with inflammatory activity.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Genotype alone does not prove amyloid deposition; different ethnic cohorts and studies have shown variable effect sizes.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: FMF + M694V/M694V + persistent inflammation or poor disease control + emerging proteinuria
Threshold / criterion status: Risk modifier, not a diagnostic threshold. Do not order MEFV testing solely as an AA screen if FMF is not otherwise suspected.

Sign / phenotype feature: Persistent/recurrent elevation of CRP or ESR
Typical timing vs diagnosis: Precedes organ manifestations if precursor disease remains active
Population / context: Known or occult chronic inflammatory condition
Quantitative / comparative evidence: AA risk tracks sustained inflammatory activity; CRP is a practical but imperfect surrogate for SAA.

Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: CRP/ESR are nonspecific and can reflect transient infection, obesity, malignancy, or other inflammatory states.

Sign / phenotype feature: Intractable or persistent diarrhea not fully explained by active IBD/infection
Population / context: Systemic AA; particularly useful outside an obvious active Crohn flare
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Japanese nationwide survey reported intractable diarrhea in 32.2% of patients at diagnosis.
Why it matters for suspicion: Adds multi-organ evidence and may indicate GI amyloid involvement.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: IBD, infection, medications, autonomic dysfunction, AL, and ATTRv can all cause chronic GI symptoms.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Persistent diarrhea + renal AA phenotype + inflammatory driver
Threshold / criterion status: No validated diarrhea duration/frequency threshold for AA screening.

Recommended use in phenotype model: Secondary supporting feature; do not trigger on diarrhea alone.

Sign / phenotype feature: Severe obesity in otherwise idiopathic AA-risk context
Population / context: Patient with persistent inflammatory phenotype or unexplained proteinuric kidney disease and no obvious classic driver
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Contemporary review notes obesity has been suggested as a cause/susceptibility factor in idiopathic AA, but mechanisms and causality remain uncertain.

Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Obesity is extremely common and strongly linked to diabetes, hypertension, obesity-related glomerulopathy, and CKD.

Sign / phenotype feature: Hypothyroidism / thyroid enlargement or goiter
Population / context: Systemic AA
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Japanese nationwide survey reported hypothyroidism in 11.6%; guidelines/reviews note thyroid deposition can occur.

Sign / phenotype feature: FMF + proteinuria with possible non-amyloid kidney disease (NAKD)
Direction for AA: AA remains possible, but proteinuria does not prove it
Population / context: FMF patients with persistent proteinuria
Quantitative / comparative evidence: In a 25-patient FMF biopsy cohort selected for proteinuria >0.5 g/day, only 15 (60%) had amyloid kidney disease; 10 (40%) had another nephropathy. Amyloid cases had heavier proteinuria (6.45 vs 2.14 g/day).

Sign / phenotype feature: Heart failure / conduction disease / cardiac imaging abnormalities in a chronic inflammatory patient
Pre-test usability: Yes if obtained for routine care

Sign / phenotype feature: Active urinary sediment / hematuria or leukocyturia in an AA-risk patient
Direction for AA: Does not exclude AA; lowers specificity
Population / context: Inflammatory/autoinflammatory patient with proteinuria
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Proteinuric FMF patients can have both amyloid and non-amyloid kidney disease; urinary sediment should therefore inform the differential rather than serve as a binary AA rule-out.
Why it matters for suspicion: Useful because simplistic 'bland sediment = amyloid, active sediment = not amyloid' logic can be unsafe.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Active sediment may favor glomerulonephritis, infection, stones, or other renal disease and therefore should reduce certainty.

Threshold / criterion status: No validated sediment cutoff for AA; do not use hematuria as either a hard rule-in or rule-out.

Recommended use in phenotype model: Uncertainty/guardrail feature, not a positive AA sign.
Ranking interpretation: Clinically important guardrail/counter-evidence; intentionally down-weighted as an AA-positive signal.

Sign / phenotype feature: No identified chronic inflammatory/infectious driver despite adequate longitudinal history
Direction for AA: Weakly argues against AA, but does not exclude it
Population / context: Patient with amyloid-like renal/systemic phenotype
Quantitative / comparative evidence: Up to roughly one-fifth of AA cases in some series/reviews are labeled idiopathic; obesity and occult inflammatory drivers may contribute.
Why it matters for suspicion: Prevents the algorithm from making a chronic inflammatory diagnosis an absolute prerequisite while still using its absence to reduce prior probability.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Occult infection, autoinflammatory disease, malignancy, or inadequately coded inflammatory disease may be missed.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: No driver + strong renal amyloid phenotype -> keep AA on broad differential but prioritize search for occult inflammation and AL/other renal causes
Threshold / criterion status: Absence of a known driver is a probabilistic down-weight, never a hard exclusion.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: no chronic inflammation; idiopathic; unexplained proteinuria
Recommended use in phenotype model: Negative modifier only.
Ranking interpretation: Clinically important guardrail/counter-evidence; intentionally down-weighted as an AA-positive signal.

Sign / phenotype feature: Known monoclonal gammopathy / plasma-cell dyscrasia in a patient with proteinuria or multisystem amyloid-like features
Direction for AA: Raises AL concern; AA remains possible
Population / context: Adult with renal/systemic phenotype
Quantitative / comparative evidence: A clonal plasma-cell context materially increases concern for AL, but MGUS can be incidental and inflammatory disease can coexist.
Why it matters for suspicion: Prevents an AA risk condition from masking a potentially urgent AL pathway.
Key overlap / mimic / guardrail: Monoclonal gammopathy is not synonymous with AL; it also occurs incidentally, especially with age.
Combination that strengthens interpretat: Monoclonal context + nephrotic proteinuria/cardiac or multisystem disease -> ensure AL work-up while retaining AA if inflammatory evidence is strong
Threshold / criterion status: No monoclonal finding should be used as an automatic AA exclusion without amyloid typing.
Example structured fields / NLP terms: MGUS; myeloma; M-protein; plasma cell dyscrasia
